awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2025 Midwest Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics Conference
awd_abstract_narration:
The Midwest Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (MTSM) Conference is a regional event that brings together early-career researchers to discuss how the behavior of tiny particles (molecules) affects things we can see and use in the real world. Topics include energy storage, environmental protection, materials design, and using biomolecules for drug delivery. The two-day event is a great chance for undergraduate students, early graduate students, and students from schools that don’t focus on research to share their work with others in the science community, without the high costs of big conferences. For many, it’s their first time at a scientific conference, which helps them improve their communication skills, expand the reach of their research, and learn new ideas and questions from others in the field. It also gives them a chance to build connections with other students, professors, and professionals from both academia and industry.

The MTSM conference promotes the exchange of new research and ideas among researchers working in different research fields whose core focus is thermodynamic behavior. Research areas include self-assembly, phase transitions, macromolecular dynamics, and macroscopic material properties, encompassing experimental, theoretical, and computational thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. The conference will comprise one keynote lecture by a senior scientist, five invited talks by early-career faculty, contributed talks from graduate students and postdocs, and contributed talks from undergraduate researchers. Participants also will be encouraged to present their work during a poster session. A point of focus for this year's invited talks will be the use of statistical mechanics to study phase behavior and transitions. Entropic forces are often crucial in the formation of materials whose molecular order is intermediate between crystals (having perfect order and reduced entropy) and liquids (having high degree of disorder and high entropy), such as liquid crystals, plastic solids, elastomers, gels, micro-segregated phases of block copolymers, and biomolecules with ordered domains like proteins. The conference will include several networking sessions to give opportunity for scientific discussion. The modest size of the MTSM conference ensures that attendees will be able to interact personally with faculty members from various research institutions, talk with other students doing similar work, and receive valuable feedback.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report: 2025 Midwest Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics Conference

The 2025 Midwest Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics Conference (MTSM) was held June 1-3, 2025, at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. With support from the National Science Foundation, the conference brought together undergraduate students (12), graduate students and postdoctoral researchers (97), and faculty (17) from across the Midwest to share recent advances in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. Participants represented a wide range of institutions, including large public universities, private research universities, and primarily undergraduate institutions.

NSF funds were used exclusively to reduce participation costs for students and early‑career researchers, substantially lowering financial barriers to attendance. This support enabled broad and equitable access to a high‑quality scientific meeting, particularly for first‑time conference attendees and participants from institutions with limited resources for travel and professional development.


Intellectual Merit

MTSM serves as a forum for presenting and discussing recent advances in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, fields that provide the theoretical foundation for understanding materials, chemical processes, and biological systems. The 2025 program featured five invited talks by early‑career faculty researchers, 25 contributed oral presentations, a keynote lecture by a senior leader in the field, and a poster session highlighting student research. Topics spanned phase behavior, molecular simulation, machine‑learning‑driven materials modeling, soft and biological materials, quantum and electronic materials, and thermodynamic equations of state.


A defining feature of MTSM is its single‑session format, which ensures that all attendees are exposed to a broad range of approaches and ideas. This structure encourages interdisciplinary engagement and allows participants to see how shared thermodynamic principles apply across different scientific problems. Survey responses (22, representative of 17% of attendees) collected six months after the conference indicate that participants found the scientific content highly valuable (rating 4.7/5.0 for quality of event). Many reported gaining exposure to new theoretical frameworks, computational tools, and modeling strategies that they have since incorporated into their own research programs.


Broader Impacts

A primary broader impact of MTSM is the professional development of students and early‑career researchers. Reduced registration and lodging costs made possible by NSF support enabled participation by individuals who might otherwise have been unable to attend a professional conference. Many students identified MTSM as their first experience presenting research in a professional setting. This early exposure builds confidence, strengthens communication skills, and helps young researchers understand how their work fits into the broader scientific landscape.Networking and community building were major outcomes of the meeting. Survey respondents reported making multiple new professional contacts and engaging in in‑depth discussions with peers and senior researchers, and gave the event a high rating for networking opportunities (4.7/5.0). Several participants described conversations that have already led to mentoring relationships, committee service, and early‑stage research collaborations, while others reported learning about new areas of research adjacent to their own. The informal and accessible nature of the conference was frequently cited as especially valuable, providing time for meaningful scientific discussions that are often difficult to achieve at large national meetings.

The conference also strengthened regional research ties by bringing together participants from institutions across the Midwest, including the University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Notre Dame, University of Michigan, Purdue University, University of Illinois Urbana‑Champaign, Northwestern University, Ohio State University, University of Minnesota, Cornell University, and others. Faculty frequently traveled with entire research groups, allowing students to benefit from both internal group mentoring and broader community engagement.

Summary

Overall, the 2025 Midwest Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics Conference successfully advanced both scientific discovery and workforce development. NSF support directly enabled student participation, expanded access to professional research dissemination, and strengthened a collaborative regional research community. Participant feedback confirms that MTSM continues to be a highly effective, low‑cost model for promoting interdisciplinary research, mentoring early‑career scientists, and sustaining the next generation of researchers in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics.
